summary: A 1971 description of the Initial Connection Protocol by A. M. McKenzie, a way for a user program to make its first connection to a service. It updates RFC 66 and RFC 80.

plainLanguage.summary: This note clears up one detail in the first connection exchange between two computers. It says to put a zero-valued type label before the 32-bit number.

subtitle: A short clarification about the first message in the Initial Connection Protocol.

tldr.problem: RFCs 66 and 80 did not make clear whether a message from Server socket 1 included a message-type code before its 32-bit number.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 93 says the Host-Host Protocol was intended to require a type code, and the documented UCSB implementation already sent code zero before the even 32-bit number.
tldr.outcome: The note recommends changing RFCs 66 and 80 to state this explicitly. Zero is the only message-type code defined at the time.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 93 as Unknown and records that it updates RFCs 66 and 80. It is a brief clarification of an early connection procedure.

sections.title: The Unclear Message
sections.content:
RFC 93 reviews the Initial Connection Protocol described in RFC 66 and restated in RFC 80. It focuses on the message sent over the connection from Server socket 1, which those documents describe as an even 32-bit number.

The text does not make clear whether the message must also begin with an eight-bit message data type code.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier instructions named a number but left out a detail. Readers could not tell whether a small type label came before it.

sections.title: What the UCSB Version Sent
sections.content:
RFC 93 says that the only documented implementation in the Network Working Group literature was at UCSB, described in RFC 74. Its implementers interpreted the Host-Host Protocol as requiring a message data type code, so they sent code zero.

This report uses that implementation as evidence about the intended message format.
sections.plainLanguage: The one documented version already included the label. It used zero as the label's value.

sections.title: The Recommended Amendment
sections.content:
Steve Crocker told the author that the Host-Host Protocol was intended to require a message data type code. The RFC therefore recommends amending RFCs 66 and 80 to say that code zero precedes the even 32-bit number.

The note adds that zero was the only code defined at that time.
sections.plainLanguage: The recommendation is to write down the intended order: first the zero code, then the number. This matches the UCSB implementation described in the note.
